title: What safety and health education must Japanese employers give new hires and transferred workers?
description: Japan hiring and change of work education: ISH Act article 59(1) and (2), the eight Ordinance article 35 items, the 2024 exemption change and dispatch.
shortAnswer: Article 59(1) and (2) of Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act require every employer to give safety and health education, without delay, to each worker it hires and to each worker whose work content changes. Article 35 of the Ordinance lists eight items. Since April 1, 2024, office based and other industries can no longer skip the four items on hazards, protective devices, work procedures and start of work checks.
keyTakeaways: Hiring education (yatoiire-ji kyōiku) and change of work education are both mandatory and must be given without delay, covering whichever of the eight article 35 items the worker's job needs.

Until March 31, 2024, workplaces in the industries grouped in item 3 of article 2 of the Enforcement Order could omit items 1 to 4; MHLW Ordinance No. 91 of 2022 removed that exemption from April 1, 2024.
For dispatched workers, the staffing agency gives hiring education, while change of work education is a duty of both the agency and the host under article 45(1) of the Worker Dispatch Act.
MHLW's guideline on employing foreign workers requires safety and health education to be delivered in a way the worker can understand, such as in the native language or with audiovisual materials.
Failing to give hiring or change of work education is punishable by a fine of up to 500,000 yen under article 120 of the Act.
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), enforced by Labor Standards Inspection Offices under each Prefectural Labor Bureau
appliesTo: Every employer in Japan that hires workers, including office based businesses such as finance, IT and professional services
Staffing agencies and host companies using dispatched workers
Line managers who reassign workers to new tasks, equipment or locations
HR, onboarding and safety teams responsible for induction programs

sections.heading: What does article 59(1) and (2) of the Industrial Safety and Health Act require?

blocks.text: Every employer must educate each worker it hires on safety or health relating to the work the worker will do, following MHLW ordinance, and must do the same when a worker's work content changes. Article 59(1) of the Industrial Safety and Health Act (労働安全衛生法, Act No. 57 of 1972) reads: "事業者は、労働者を雇い入れたときは、当該労働者に対し、厚生労働省令で定めるところにより、その従事する業務に関する安全又は衛生のための教育を行なわなければならない。" Article 59(2) applies the same rule "when the work content of a worker has changed" ([Industrial Safety and Health Act, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347AC0000000057)).

The Act does not distinguish full time, part time, fixed term or short term workers in this article; the trigger is the hiring itself. Change of work education is triggered by a change in what the worker does, such as a new machine, process, chemical or workplace, rather than by a change of job title. This page describes the duty as at November 2026. The other education duties under the Act, including special education and foreman education, are summarized in [what Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act requires](/regulations/japan-industrial-safety-and-health-act-training).

sections.heading: What must hiring and change of work education cover?

blocks.text: Article 35(1) of the Ordinance on Industrial Safety and Health (労働安全衛生規則, Ministry of Labor Ordinance No. 32 of 1972) requires the employer to educate the worker "遅滞なく" (without delay) on whichever of eight items are necessary for safety or health in that worker's job ([Ordinance, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347M50002000032)). The table groups them by whether they were previously exempt.

blocks.text: Article 35(2) still lets the employer omit an item for an individual worker who is recognized as having sufficient knowledge and skill in it. That is a person based judgment, not an industry based one, and it should be documented with the reason.

sections.heading: What changed for office based industries on April 1, 2024?

blocks.text: Industries that could previously skip items 1 to 4 must now cover them wherever they are relevant to the job. Article 2 of the Order for Enforcement of the Industrial Safety and Health Act sorts industries into three groups: (1) forestry, mining, construction, transport and cleaning; (2) manufacturing, utilities, communications, certain wholesale and retail trades, hotels, golf courses, automobile maintenance and machinery repair; and (3) "その他の業種", all other industries ([Enforcement Order, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347CO0000000318)). The old proviso to article 35 allowed group 3 workplaces to omit items 1 to 4.

MHLW Ordinance No. 91 of 2022 deleted that proviso as part of the chemical management reforms. The implementation circular states that the amendment extended the industries covered by items 1 to 4 to all industries, that the content of the education is unchanged, and that newly covered industries must deliver the education needed according to each workplace's work ([MHLW implementation circular Kihatsu 0531 No. 9](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11300000/000987120.pdf)). MHLW's overview of the reforms gives the start date as April 1, 2024 ([MHLW chemical regulation overview](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11300000/001083280.pdf)).

blocks.title: What this means for an office
blocks.text: The change does not oblige an office to invent machine hazards. It removes the blanket permission to skip items 1 to 4. Where office staff use cleaning chemicals, toner, kitchen equipment, ladders, data center equipment or electrically powered tools, the hazards, protective devices, procedures and pre use checks for those items now need to be covered in hiring education.

sections.heading: Who educates dispatched workers, and how must foreign workers be taught?

blocks.text: The staffing agency, as the employer, gives hiring education to a dispatched worker. For change of work education, article 45(1) of the Worker Dispatch Act (Act No. 88 of 1985) deems the host to be an employer as well, applying article 59(2) to both parties ([Worker Dispatch Act, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/360AC0000000088)). In practice the agency covers general content before dispatch and the host covers the site's machinery, procedures, start of work checks and evacuation routes, because only the host knows them. Special education for listed hazardous operations sits with the host alone, as explained in [Japan's special education for hazardous work](/regulations/japan-special-education-for-hazardous-work).

For foreign workers, the Guideline for Employers on Improving Employment Management of Foreign Workers (MHLW Notice No. 276 of 2007) states that when giving safety and health education required by the Industrial Safety and Health Act, the employer must use a method the worker can understand, for example by using the native language or audiovisual materials (母国語等を用いる、視聴覚教材を用いる等), taking particular care that the hazards of machinery and raw materials and how to handle them are understood ([MHLW foreign worker employment guideline](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/000601382.pdf)). The guideline also asks employers to endeavor to teach the Japanese and basic signals needed to follow accident prevention instructions.

sections.heading: Must hiring education be recorded, and what are the penalties?

blocks.text: Article 35 contains no record keeping rule, unlike the three year record required for special education. Breach of article 59(1), including as applied by article 59(2), is nevertheless punishable under article 120 of the Act by a fine of up to 500,000 yen, and article 122 extends the fine to the company. Without a record, an employer has little way to show an inspector that education was given without delay or which items were covered.

A defensible record captures the date, the worker, the items delivered against the eight in article 35(1), any item omitted under article 35(2) with the reason, the instructor and the language of delivery for foreign workers. For retention periods, see [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

sections.heading: How should a hiring education program be built and evidenced?

blocks.text: Build the content per role and per site, not as one corporate video, because article 35 asks for the items needed in the worker's own job. The mapping below is illustrative good practice; only the triggers, the eight items and the dispatch allocation come from law.

Where chemicals are involved, the content should be planned with the site's [chemical substance manager](/regulations/japan-chemical-substance-manager-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each of the eight article 35 items to the hazards present in each role and site, so hiring and change of work education can be generated from the same framework and every omission is traceable to a recorded reason. When the law removed the industry exemption in 2024, that structure showed exactly which roles needed items 1 to 4 added.

faqs.q: Is there a minimum number of hours for hiring education in Japan?
faqs.a: No. Article 35 of the Ordinance sets content and timing but no minimum hours, unlike special education and foreman education. The time needed depends on the hazards of the job, so a desk role and a warehouse role may need very different programs.

faqs.q: Does a worker transferring between two sites of the same company need education again?
faqs.a: If the work content changes, yes. Article 59(2) is triggered by a change in the work, so a transfer that brings new equipment, procedures, chemicals or evacuation arrangements requires change of work education on those points, even if the job title stays the same.

faqs.q: Can hiring education be delivered online?
faqs.a: Yes, provided it covers the items the job needs and the employer can confirm the worker actually completed it. MHLW's circular on e-learning, last revised on September 2, 2026, sets those conditions for statutory safety and health education delivered over the internet.

faqs.q: Did the April 2024 change require retraining existing staff?
faqs.a: The article 35 change applies at hiring and on a change of work, so it bites on new hires and reassignments from April 1, 2024. Employers that relied on the old exemption may still choose to cover items 1 to 4 for existing staff to keep records consistent.

factCheck.claim: Article 59(1) requires education on hiring per MHLW ordinance; 59(2) applies it on a change of work content; article 120 punishes breach of 59(1) including as applied by 59(2) with a fine up to 500,000 yen; article 122 adds corporate fines.

Ordinance article 35(1) requires education without delay (遅滞なく) on hiring or change of work on the needed items among eight listed; 35(2) allows omission for a worker with sufficient knowledge and skill; article 35 has no record keeping rule while article 38 requires 3 year special education records.

Enforcement Order article 2 groups industries as (1) forestry, mining, construction, transport, cleaning; (2) manufacturing, electricity, gas, heat supply, water, communications, listed wholesale and retail, hotels, golf courses, automobile maintenance, machinery repair; (3) other industries.

Workplaces in Order article 2 item 3 industries could previously omit Ordinance article 35(1) items 1 to 4; MHLW Ordinance No. 91 of 2022 deleted the omission, extending items 1 to 4 to all industries with unchanged content, and newly covered industries must educate according to each workplace's work.
The hiring education industry omission was abolished from April 1, 2024.
Worker Dispatch Act article 45(1) deems the host also an employer for ISH Act 59(2), while 59(1) is not applied to the host; 59(3) is applied to the host under 45(3).

MHLW Notice No. 276 of 2007 (foreign worker guideline), section on safety and health: employers must deliver ISH Act safety and health education in a way the foreign worker understands, such as native language or audiovisual materials, ensuring hazards and handling of machinery and raw materials are understood, and endeavor to teach necessary Japanese and basic signals.
